newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan Central Bank takes over Amman Investment Bank.
newsitem.headline: Jordan Central Bank takes over Amman Investment Bank.

text.p: Jordan's Central Bank has taken control of troubled Amman Investment Bank to help restore its finances ahead of an anticipated takeover by another bank, bankers said on Tuesday.
Banking sources said a seven man committee headed by senior Central Bank official Ahmad Abdel-Fattah was now charged with the day-to-day supervision and management of the bank.
The decision, which was taken in a board meeting of the Central Bank on Saturday, effectively puts the loss-making bank, one of Jordan's six investment banks, under its custody.

"Jordan Central Bank board has decided under its decision taken on March 1 to appoint a committee headed by Ahmad Abdel-Fattah, the assistant governor, with the committee enjoying full jurisdiction in supervision over the bank and its management," a Central Bank document seen by Reuters said.

Amman Investment Bank, whose total assets stood at 111.1 million dinars ($157 million) at the end of 1995, has accumulated losses which stood at 32 million dinars according to latest published statements.
Bankers say the losses include doubtful loans of 23.3 million dinars, out of a total 63 million dinar loan portfolio.

Bankers say the bank, created by a merger of financial and industrial firms in 1982, had been burdened with bad debts of 11 million dinars inherited from Industrial Investments, Finance and Credit, and the Jordanian Company for Leasing of Equipment.
The bank's former management had been in talks with the Central Bank on acquisition terms with a number of banks, including Jordan's leading Arab Bank and Cairo-Amman Bank .
Arab Bank, the main contender to buy the bank, has been primarily interested in using the bank's license to operate an Islamic banking unit, bankers say.

The Central Bank has practically stopped issuing bank licenses in what it views as an overcrowded banking market with 20 private banks. It has been prodding banks to merge by raising capital ceilings and offering incentives, part of its overall strategy of creating a stronger banking system.
Bankers say the onus will be on the Central Bank to come out with a strategy to restructure the bank and find a buyer to inject new capital after cleaning it up.
They shrugged off any negative impact on the Jordanian banking sector's confidence, saying the move was long overdue in light of Amman Investment Bank's long-simmering bad debt problems.
It enhanced confidence in the monetary authorities readiness to act when it was required to bolster the sector, they said.
The Central Bank's intervention is the third in the country's banking history after it liquidated Petra Bank in 1989 and helped restructure Jordan-Gulf Bank in 1993.

The latest Central Bank move comes after shareholders failed to raise the bank's capital, which had slipped to five million from 15 million dinars, up to the 20 million dinars minimum level imposed by the Central Bank.
The bank, which pursued an aggressive policy in equity and direct investments, built up a large investment portfolio.

Amman Investment Bank has stakes in Mafraq Food Industries company (MAFICO), Rum Metal Manufacturing Company, Arab Electrical Industries, Jordan Spinning and Weaving, Ahliyah Metal Industries, and Amman Casting Company.
The bank's major shareholders included leading Jordanian-Palestinian businessman Sabih al-Masri, who owns 25 percent, and the government pension fund, which owns around 10 percent.
